name: Hospitality
core_perception: The audience is buying an anticipated experience of a place, so the work must make a specific location feel both desirable and real. Generic luxury imagery is actively counterproductive because the buyer is trying to judge whether this particular place suits them.
visual_traits: environmental photography with strong sense of place
material and texture detail at close range
restrained typography that does not compete with the space
communication_needs: establish the specific character of the place
show the experience rather than the facilities list
make practical information easy to find
composition: Image-led with generous space and quiet type. Wide establishing views paired with intimate detail shots is the strongest pattern, because the audience needs both the promise and the evidence.
typography: Understated and well-spaced, frequently a refined serif or a quiet neutral sans. Type should feel like signage within the space rather than advertising laid over it.
color: Drawn from the actual materials and light of the property. Imposed brand colour that contradicts the physical space undermines the credibility of the whole piece.
imagery: Real light at real times of day. Empty perfect rooms feel sterile; traces of use, food, hands and movement make a space feel inhabitable.
avoid: Interchangeable luxury imagery that could belong to any property in any country, which defeats the specificity the category sells on.
Dense promotional overlays on environmental photography, which convert an aspirational image into a discount advertisement.
Heavy graphic treatment competing with the architecture and light of the space itself.
